chapter.name: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

questions.q: Which statement about the states of water is correct?
questions.a: Changes of state of water form no new substance.
o: Water changes between solid, liquid and gas by physical changes
Water turning to ice forms a new substance because ice is hard
Boiling water is a chemical change because steam escapes into the air
Only ice melting is physical; steam turning back to water is a chemical change

questions.q: Make up two changes that could happen in a school canteen, one physical and one not physical. Name each and justify with the new-substance test.
questions.a: e.g. Cutting a cake is physical (size and shape only). Burning gas in a stove is not physical because new substances form.

questions.q: At a school tuck shop, the helper chops onions, boils water for tea, burns wood in the stove and lights a kerosene lamp. Which pair contains only physical changes?
questions.a: Burning wood is chemical; each wrong pair includes it.
o: Chopping onions and boiling water
Boiling water and burning wood
Chopping onions and burning wood
Burning wood and lighting the kerosene lamp

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a physical change?
questions.a: Burning wood forms new substances; the other three change only state, size or shape.
o: Burning wood in a chulha
Boiling water for tea
Cutting paper into strips for a collage
Chopping vegetables for a sabzi

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Drying wet clothes
2. Crushing chalk
3. Burning wood
4. Folding paper
A. Shape changes; the paper is still paper
B. Water changes from liquid to gas
C. New substances are formed
D. The size reduces to a fine powder
questions.a: Drying clothes: water to gas (B); chalk: powder (D); burning wood: new substances (C); folding paper: shape (A).

questions.q:
A class table lists: boiling water, chopping vegetables, drying wet clothes, burning kerosene and melting ice.
(a) Name the physical changes.
(b) For each, say whether the property that changes is shape, size or state.
(c) Explain why the remaining change is different.
(d) State the test that settles any such case.
questions.a: Physical: boiling water (state), chopping vegetables (size, shape), drying clothes (state), melting ice (state). Burning kerosene forms new substances. Test: is a new substance formed?
s: Names the property changed in each

questions.q: Which of these is a physical change?
questions.a: Melting changes only the state. The other three form new substances (burning gives combustion products; rust is iron oxide).
o: Melting a cube of ice in a glass
Burning a heap of dry kerosene-soaked cotton
Rusting of an iron cycle chain in the rain
Burning a strip of magnesium ribbon

questions.q:
For Diwali, Meera crushed coloured chalk into powder for a rangoli. Her brother folded sheets of paper into lanterns and she deflated balloons that had hung overnight. She is making a chart with two columns, 'physical' and 'chemical'. Her cousin wants to add 'burning a wooden splint to light the diya'.
(a) Which column does crushing chalk go in, and why?
(b) What stays the same in the chalk, paper and balloon?
(c) Which column does burning the wooden splint go in?
(d) Her brother says he can only enter a change in the 'physical' column if it can be undone. Decide whether he is right.
questions.a: (a) Physical: size changes only. (b) The material. (c) Chemical: new substances form. (d) Wrong: physical changes need not be reversible; use the new-substance test.
s: Part (b): the material stays the same
Part (d): rejects reversibility as the test

questions.q:
Read the statements about physical changes.
I. A change of state of a substance always produces a new substance.
II. Crushing a piece of chalk gives a powder that is still chalk.
III. Chopped vegetables are the same vegetables, only smaller.
questions.a: I is false: a change of state forms no new substance. II and III are true.
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
A steel tumbler of water is kept in a freezer and becomes ice. The ice is later left outside and becomes water again.
(a) Name the type of change.
(b) What does the return of water tell you about the substance?
questions.a: (a) Physical change. (b) It is the same substance (water) in a different state; no new substance formed.
s: Part (b): the same substance returns, so no new substance formed

questions.q: Gauri says: 'Drying wet clothes and melting ice are both physical changes because in each the water only changes its state.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. In drying, water goes from liquid to gas; in melting, from solid to liquid. No new substance forms in either, so both are physical.
s: Explains the state change in each

questions.q:
Plan a 'physical change corner' for the science fair using three household items.
(a) Name three activities.
(b) For each, say what changes and what stays the same.
(c) Say how a visitor can tell that no new substance formed.
(d) Add one care you will take.
questions.a: e.g. folding paper (shape; still paper), crushing chalk (size; still chalk), inflating a balloon (shape; still rubber). No new substance means material is unchanged. Care with pins.
s: Method to tell no new substance formed

questions.q: A physical change is best described as a change in which
questions.a: Book definition. Reversibility and heat are not part of it; the last wrong option describes combustion.
o: no new substance forms; only shape, size or state changes
a new substance forms, but it looks the same as the old one
the change happens suddenly and can never be reversed
the substance is heated until it gives out heat and light

questions.q: Making a paper boat, drying wet clothes, burning cotton and crushing chalk are listed. Which are physical changes? Give the common reason, and say why the other is not.
questions.a: Physical: paper boat, drying clothes, crushing chalk. No new substance forms. Burning cotton forms new substances.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Boiling water is a chemical change.
Reason (R): Boiling changes water from liquid to gas without forming a new substance.
questions.a: A is false: boiling is a physical change. R is a true fact, but it contradicts A.
o: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false

questions.q:
Water in a pan is heated until it boils away.
(a) Name the two states of water involved.
(b) Explain why this is a physical change.
questions.a: (a) Liquid and gas. (b) Only the state changes; no new substance forms.
s: Part (b): no new substance, state change only

questions.q: Define a physical change and give two examples of changes around you that are physical.
questions.a: A change in which only physical properties like shape, size or state change and no new substance forms. Examples: cutting paper, boiling water.

questions.q: A mango in a bowl smells stronger next day and shows dark spots. Name the two senses a student uses to notice this and say what each detects.
questions.a: Sight detects the dark spots; smell detects the stronger smell.

questions.q: For a fancy-dress show, Zoya folds a newspaper into a hat and later flattens it again. What does the creased sheet show?
questions.a: A change of shape alone is a physical change; the material stays the same.
o: It is still paper; only its shape changed
Folding formed a new substance that cannot be undone
Creases are signs of a chemical change in paper
The paper lost mass, so it is no longer paper

questions.q:
On Sports Day, Mr Khan put 12 ice cubes in a bucket of water for the runners' bottles. By the end of the first race the cubes were gone. A volunteer chopped 30 oranges for the interval. Rahul says chopped oranges cannot be put back together. Priya says chopping is a physical change.
(a) Name the type of change the ice cubes went through and the two states involved.
(b) Does chopping form a new substance? Explain.
(c) The bibs on the rope were wet; where did the water go?
(d) Can Rahul and Priya both be right? Decide.
questions.a: (a) Physical; solid to liquid. (b) No; only size and shape change. (c) It changed to gas (evaporated), a physical change. (d) Yes: chopping is physical but cannot be reversed.
s: Part (d): both right; physical changes need not be reversible

questions.q: Differentiate between a change of shape and a change of state, with one example of each.
questions.a: Shape: form alters, e.g. folding a sheet. State: solid, liquid or gas changes, e.g. ice melting. Both are physical.

questions.q: A hostel warden hangs wet towels on the terrace in the morning and finds them dry by evening. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Drying wet clothes is a state change of water from liquid to gas: physical.
o: Water changed from liquid to gas, so it is a physical change
The cotton changed into another substance as the towels lost weight
The water reacted with sunlight, so it is a chemical change
Water changed from gas to liquid, a physical change

questions.q: The milkiness of lime water after exhaled air is blown into it is due to
questions.a: Carbon dioxide and calcium hydroxide form insoluble calcium carbonate (plus a little water), which makes the liquid look milky.
o: calcium carbonate, which does not dissolve
calcium hydroxide separating out from the water
carbon dioxide bubbles trapped inside the liquid
tiny droplets of water from the breath settling

questions.q:
In the science club, Nisha added a spoon of baking soda to lemon juice in a bottle. She connected a straw to a second bottle holding freshly prepared lime water and watched it. Her brother Aarav repeated the activity with baking soda and plain water. Aarav suggests using plain water in place of lime water in the second bottle because it costs nothing.
(a) Name the gas that formed in Nisha's first bottle and the evidence in the second bottle.
(b) What difference will Aarav see in his first bottle, and why?
(c) Write the word equation for the change in the lime water bottle.
(d) Decide whether plain water can replace lime water, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Carbon dioxide; lime water turns milky. (b) No bubbles with plain water; no reaction. (c) Calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide gives calcium carbonate + water. (d) No: plain water shows only bubbles, never the milkiness that identifies the gas.
s: Part (a): carbon dioxide with milky lime water
Part (b): no bubbles with plain water
Part (d): no, plain water cannot identify the gas

questions.q: Four cups of lime water each receive the gas from a different mixture: (i) vinegar and baking soda, (ii) lemon juice and baking soda, (iii) baking soda and plain water, (iv) exhaled air blown into plain tap water instead of lime water. In which cups of lime water does the gas turn it milky?
questions.a: Acid with baking soda gives carbon dioxide; baking soda with plain water gives no bubbles; (iv) never touches lime water.
o: (i) and (ii) only
(i) and (iii) only
(ii) and (iii) only
(iii) and (iv) only

questions.q:
At the Annual Day science stall, visitors blew through straws into two cups: cup A had tap water and cup B had lime water. Volunteer Kabir left both cups on the table for half an hour. A visitor wants to blow into cup A twenty times to make it turn milky, while Kabir says that will not work.
(a) What would visitors see in each cup right after blowing?
(b) What will cup B show after half an hour, and what does it prove?
(c) Which cup is the comparison cup, and what does it show?
(d) Decide who is right about blowing twenty times into cup A.
questions.a: (a) A: bubbles; B: bubbles and milkiness. (b) A white layer settles: new substance formed. (c) Cup A shows bubbles alone do not give milkiness. (d) Kabir: tap water has no calcium hydroxide, so it only bubbles.
s: Part (a): correct observation in A and B
Part (b): settled white substance shows a new substance
Part (d): Kabir is right with reason

questions.q:
A pinch of baking soda is added to lemon juice.
(a) What do you observe?
(b) What will this gas do to freshly prepared lime water and what does that tell you about it?
questions.a: (a) A fizzing sound and gas bubbles. (b) It turns lime water milky, so it is carbon dioxide.
s: Part (b): milky lime water shows carbon dioxide

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a chemical change?
questions.a: Tap water shows bubbles only and no new substance. The others each form a new substance.
o: Blowing air through a straw into tap water
Exhaled air turning a tumbler of lime water milky
Lemon juice fizzing when baking soda is added
Vinegar fizzing when baking soda is added

questions.q: Differentiate between what is seen when exhaled air is blown into tap water and into lime water.
questions.a: Tap water: bubbles only, no change in appearance. Lime water: bubbles and milkiness, because a new substance forms.

questions.q: Show that the milkiness of lime water cannot be explained by bubbles alone.
questions.a: Tap water also gets bubbles from the same breath but stays clear. In lime water a white substance settles, so a new substance formed.
s: Settled white substance in lime water

questions.q: Which observation shows that a chemical change has taken place?
questions.a: A new substance (settling white solid) shows a chemical change. Bubbles alone, as in tap water, do not.
o: A white substance settles out of a liquid
Bubbles rise in the liquid
The liquid is poured into a smaller glass
The liquid takes the shape of its container

questions.q:
Exhaled air is blown into lime water.
(a) Write the word equation for the reaction.
(b) Why is this a chemical change and not a physical one?
questions.a: (a) Calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide gives calcium carbonate + water. (b) A new substance, calcium carbonate, forms.

questions.q: A tumbler of lime water has turned milky. Write two different ways in which the gas that did this could have been produced.
questions.a: Blowing exhaled air into it; vinegar or lemon juice with baking soda, passing the gas into it.
s: First valid source of carbon dioxide
Links the gas to the milky test

questions.q: What is the test for carbon dioxide gas?
questions.a: Only lime water turning milky is the test. Bubbles in tap water or fizzing do not identify the gas.
o: It turns lime water milky
It makes tap water bubble when passed through it
It makes a fizzing sound when it forms
It turns tap water cloudy when blown into it

questions.q: What is a chemical reaction? How can it be written in short form?
questions.a: The process by which new substances form in a chemical change; it is written as a chemical equation (reactants give products).
s: Chemical reaction as formation of new substances

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Milky lime water is used as a test for carbon dioxide.
Reason (R): Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide in lime water to form calcium carbonate.
questions.a: Both are true and the reaction explains why milkiness is the sign of carbon dioxide.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: After exhaled air is blown into a tumbler of lime water, the liquid is left overnight and a white layer is found at the bottom. Which reason is correct?
questions.a: The insoluble calcium carbonate settles, which shows a new substance formed.
o: Calcium carbonate, a new substance, does not dissolve and settles
Calcium hydroxide has simply separated out of the water on standing
Carbon dioxide has condensed into a solid layer at the bottom of it
Some of the water has evaporated and left a dry solid behind

questions.q: Ritu adds a pinch of baking soda to lemon juice in a small bottle and passes the gas through a straw into a second bottle of freshly prepared lime water. What will she see?
questions.a: Lemon juice with baking soda gives carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky.
o: Fizzing in the first bottle and the lime water turning milky
No change in the first bottle and milky lime water
Fizzing in the first bottle but clear lime water, as the gas is air
Fizzing in both bottles with the lime water staying clear

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Lime water
2. Calcium carbonate
3. Vinegar with baking soda
4. Baking soda with plain water
A. Fizzing, and carbon dioxide forms
B. White substance that does not dissolve in water
C. Solution of calcium hydroxide used to test for carbon dioxide
D. No bubbles are seen
questions.a: Lime water: calcium hydroxide solution (C); calcium carbonate: insoluble white substance (B); vinegar and soda: fizzing and carbon dioxide (A); soda and water: no bubbles (D).

questions.q: Imran says: 'The gas from lemon juice and baking soda is the same gas as in our breath, because both turn lime water milky.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. Both turn lime water milky, which is the test for carbon dioxide, so both are carbon dioxide. (Same test result shows same gas.)
s: Milky lime water is the test for carbon dioxide

questions.q: Name the gas that is tested with lime water, and the new white substance that forms and makes the liquid look milky.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide; calcium carbonate.

questions.q:
Three tumblers: P holds tap water and Q holds lime water, both with exhaled air blown in; R holds lime water receiving gas from vinegar and baking soda.
(a) Predict what is seen in each.
(b) Name the gas in Q and in R.
(c) Say whether the changes are physical or chemical, with a reason.
(d) State why P is a useful comparison.
questions.a: P: only bubbles; Q: milky; R: milky. Carbon dioxide in both. Q and R are chemical changes (new substance). P shows bubbles alone do not mean a chemical change.
s: Predicts P, Q and R correctly
Names carbon dioxide for Q and R

questions.q:
Design an investigation to find out whether the gas from lemon juice and baking soda is carbon dioxide.
(a) List the materials.
(b) Write the steps, with one safety caution.
(c) State the observation and what it proves.
(d) Write the word equation for the confirming reaction.
questions.a: Lemon juice, baking soda, test tubes, lime water, flexible straw. Add soda to juice, pass gas through straw into lime water; do not suck. Milky shows carbon dioxide. Calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide gives calcium carbonate + water.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the lime water test.
I. Exhaled air contains carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky.
II. Baking soda added to plain water gives bubbles of carbon dioxide.
III. Calcium carbonate is formed, along with a little water, in the lime water test.
questions.a: II is false: baking soda with plain water gives no bubbles.
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
In the school lab, Ms Rao held a magnesium ribbon with tongs and lit it in open air. It burned with a bright white light, and a white powder was left. For a demonstration to the whole class, a student suggests burning the ribbon inside a tightly closed glass jar so that nobody gets close to the flame.
(a) Name the white powder and write the word equation.
(b) Classify the change and justify.
(c) Is it combustion? Explain.
(d) Decide whether the closed jar is a good plan for the demonstration.
questions.a: (a) Magnesium oxide; magnesium + oxygen gives magnesium oxide + heat + light. (b) Chemical, new substance. (c) Yes: reacts with oxygen producing heat and light. (d) Not a good plan: in a closed jar the supply of air runs out, so the burning would stop.
s: Part (b): chemical with new substance reason
Part (d): closed jar lacks continuous air supply

questions.q: On a field trip, students see small insects glowing near a bush after sunset. Their teacher says the light comes from a chemical change. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Fireflies make light by a chemical change without heat: bioluminescence.
o: It is bioluminescence: light made without heat
It is combustion, in which the insects burn a wax-like vapour inside
It is a physical change, as the insects only reflect the moonlight
It is combustion, so the insects also give out a lot of heat

questions.q: Define combustion and give two combustible substances.
questions.a: A reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen producing heat and/or light. Examples: wood, kerosene.

questions.q:
Iron nails left in damp air turn brown.
(a) Name the brown substance.
(b) Why can we say rust is a different substance from iron?
questions.a: (a) Rust, iron oxide. (b) It is a new substance with different appearance, formed in a chemical change.
s: Part (a): names rust or iron oxide
Part (b): new substance, so a chemical change

questions.q: Rusting of iron is a chemical change because
questions.a: Rust is a new substance, iron oxide.
o: a new brown substance, iron oxide, forms
the nail loses its shape while it turns brown
heat and light are given out as the iron changes colour
the iron changes from a solid into a liquid state

questions.q: A lab has a magnesium ribbon, an iron nail left in damp air and a candle. For each, state whether it undergoes a chemical change and name one new substance formed.
questions.a: Magnesium: magnesium oxide. Iron nail: rust (iron oxide). Candle: carbon dioxide (from carbon of wax and oxygen).

questions.q: Dev says: 'Whenever light is made by a chemical change, heat must also be given out.' Do you agree? Give an example from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Fireflies make light by a chemical change without heat (bioluminescence).

questions.q: A woman's cotton dupatta catches fire in a kitchen. A neighbour has a thick cotton blanket and a synthetic bedsheet. What should she do first?
questions.a: Cutting off the air puts out the fire; synthetic cloth should not be used as it can melt and stick to the skin.
o: Wrap the cotton blanket around her to cut off the air
Wrap the synthetic bedsheet tightly because it covers more
Tell her to run to the door so the air blows the flames out
Wave the burning dupatta to fan the flames away from her

questions.q: A group wants to keep a candle burning for a full hour under an inverted glass tumbler. Show why this cannot work.
questions.a: Oxygen supports combustion; the covered candle has no continuous supply of air, so the oxygen runs out and the flame goes out; carbon dioxide forms.
s: No continuous air supply under the tumbler
Flame goes out; carbon dioxide forms

questions.q: Two identical oil lamps (diyas) are lit in a hall. A steel bowl is placed upside down over one of them. What happens and why?
questions.a: Oxygen in air supports combustion; under the bowl the supply of air runs out.
o: The covered lamp goes out soon as its air supply stops
The covered lamp goes out because the steel bowl cools its flame down
The open lamp goes out first because it loses its heat to the whole room
Both keep burning for long because oxygen is not needed for burning

questions.q: What is bioluminescence? Name one living thing that shows it and say how its light differs from that of a burning candle.
questions.a: Light production by a chemical change without heat in living organisms. Firefly. A candle gives out heat along with light.
s: Names the firefly and contrasts with heat in the candle

questions.q:
A magnesium ribbon and a candle are both burnt.
(a) Write the reactants and products of burning magnesium.
(b) State where the carbon dioxide from the candle comes from.
(c) Give one sign that each is a chemical change.
(d) State one thing both need.
questions.a: Magnesium + oxygen gives magnesium oxide + heat + light. Carbon dioxide forms from carbon in wax and oxygen. New substances (magnesium oxide; carbon dioxide). Both need oxygen.
s: Carbon of wax plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide
New substance as sign for each

questions.q:
A candle goes out under an inverted tumbler.
(a) Which gas supports combustion?
(b) After the flame goes out, how will you show that carbon dioxide has formed inside the tumbler?
questions.a: (a) Oxygen. (b) Add a little lime water in the petri dish; it turns milky.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A candle covered with a glass tumbler goes out after some time.
Reason (R): Carbon dioxide is formed from the carbon in the wax and the oxygen of the air.
questions.a: A is true because the air supply is limited. R is true but describes a product; it does not explain why the flame goes out.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: When a magnesium ribbon burns in air, the substance formed is
questions.a: Magnesium + oxygen gives magnesium oxide + heat + light.
o: magnesium oxide, a white powder
iron oxide, a brown substance like rust
calcium carbonate, the white substance from lime water
magnesium carbonate, a gas that turns lime water milky

questions.q: Combustion is a reaction in which a substance
questions.a: Book definition; the wrong options describe a water reaction, melting and a physical change.
o: reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and/or light
reacts with water and gives out only heat to its surroundings
melts when heat is supplied and returns to a solid on cooling
changes its state without forming any new substance at all

questions.q:
On a camping trip, students lit a diya at dusk and covered it with a steel tumbler to shield it from wind. The flame went out soon. Later they saw fireflies glowing near the tents. The camp leader wants to keep one blanket ready in case anyone's clothes catch fire. A synthetic one is lighter to carry; a cotton one is heavier.
(a) Why did the diya flame go out?
(b) How could you show that a gas formed under the tumbler?
(c) How does firefly light differ from the diya's light?
(d) Decide which blanket to keep and justify.
questions.a: (a) The air supply under the tumbler ran out; oxygen is needed. (b) Lime water turns milky for carbon dioxide. (c) Firefly: chemical change without heat; diya: combustion with heat. (d) Cotton: synthetic can melt and stick to skin, even though it is lighter.
s: Part (c): light without heat vs combustion
Part (d): cotton chosen with the melting reason

questions.q:
A magnesium ribbon is burnt in air.
(a) Write the word equation.
(b) Name the two forms of energy given out and say what they show about the change.
questions.a: (a) Magnesium + oxygen gives magnesium oxide + heat + light. (b) Heat and light; it is combustion.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a combustible substance?
questions.a: Cotton, paper and kerosene burn; glass does not undergo combustion.
o: A glass bottle
A cotton cloth
A sheet of paper
Kerosene in a lamp

questions.q:
Two groups cover a burning candle with inverted tumblers: Group A uses a small tumbler, Group B uses a large one.
(a) Predict what happens in each.
(b) Explain the reason.
(c) State which flame lasts longer and why.
(d) Name the test that shows carbon dioxide in each tumbler.
questions.a: Both flames go out; the large tumbler holds more air so the flame lasts longer; oxygen runs out; lime water turns milky.
s: Explains the air supply runs out
Large tumbler lasts longer because more air

questions.q:
Read the statements about burning and rusting.
I. Burning a magnesium ribbon forms magnesium oxide and gives out heat and light.
II. Rusting of iron forms the new substance iron oxide.
III. Combustion can go on without oxygen if the substance is hot enough.
questions.a: III is false: oxygen is essential for combustion.
o: Statements I and II only
Statements II and III only
Statements I and III only
Statements I, II and III

questions.q: Differentiate between the ignition temperature of paper and the temperature of a lighted matchstick, and say how they are related.
questions.a: Ignition temperature is the minimum temperature at which paper catches fire; the match's temperature is already higher than it, so paper burns at once.
s: Match's temperature higher, so paper burns at once

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Fuel
2. Oxygen
3. Ignition temperature
4. Lighted matchstick
A. Part of air that supports combustion
B. Already hotter than the ignition temperature of paper
C. Minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire
D. A combustible substance such as wood or paper
questions.a: Fuel: combustible substance (D); oxygen: part of air (A); ignition temperature: minimum temperature (C); lighted match: hotter than paper's (B).

questions.q: Which set lists the three requirements for combustion?
questions.a: The fire triangle. A flame is not essential, as the magnifying glass activity shows.
o: Fuel, oxygen and heat to reach ignition temperature
Fuel, water and a strong source of heat
Fuel, oxygen and a naked flame in contact with it
Oxygen, heat and a supply of carbon dioxide

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Paper can be set on fire using a magnifying glass and sunlight.
Reason (R): Focusing the sunrays lowers the ignition temperature of the paper.
questions.a: A is true: the paper is heated until it catches fire. R is false: the ignition temperature does not change; the paper is heated up to it.
o: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: Kavya says: 'A substance can burn without a flame touching it.' Is she right? What more must she add to be complete?
questions.a: Yes, e.g. paper burns under focused sunrays. She must add that the substance needs oxygen and must be heated to its ignition temperature.
s: Verdict: right, with the sunray evidence

questions.q: Neha focuses sunrays with a lens to the smallest, brightest spot on a page torn from an old notebook. After a while it smokes and then burns. Which explanation is correct?
questions.a: Heating raised the paper's temperature until it reached the ignition temperature.
o: The sunrays, focused, heated the page to its ignition temperature
The lens supplied extra oxygen to the page from the air
The lens made a flame of its own that burnt the page
The ignition temperature of paper fell down to room temperature

questions.q:
(a) Define ignition temperature.
(b) Why did a lighted matchstick set paper on fire almost immediately?
questions.a: (a) The minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire. (b) The match is already hotter than the paper's ignition temperature.
s: Part (b): match is hotter than paper's ignition temperature

questions.q:
Four trials: (i) paper kept on a desk; (ii) a stone held near a lighted matchstick; (iii) paper held to a lighted matchstick; (iv) paper held in a flame inside a sealed jar whose oxygen has all been used.
(a) Predict whether a fire occurs in each.
(b) Name the missing side of the fire triangle in each trial without a fire.
(c) State what the trial with fire has.
questions.a: (i) no, heat is missing; (ii) no, fuel is missing; (iii) yes, all three; (iv) no, oxygen is missing.
s: Predicts the outcome in each trial

questions.q:
(a) Why is the sunray spot made the smallest and brightest?
(b) What does the paper do before it catches fire?
questions.a: (a) To concentrate the heat so the paper's temperature rises. (b) It emits smoke.

questions.q: The minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire is called its
questions.a: Book term: ignition temperature.
o: ignition temperature
melting temperature of the fuel
flame temperature of the match
boiling temperature of the fuel

questions.q:
At the science exhibition, Manju held a sheet of newspaper with tongs and focused sunrays on it with a magnifying glass. Zoya held a lighted matchstick to another sheet. The teacher says she can allow only one of the two activities for the Class 5 visitors, and wants the choice justified.
(a) Which requirement of combustion does each activity supply as the heat source?
(b) Which sheet will burn sooner, and why?
(c) What is common to both activities for the paper to burn?
(d) Decide which activity to allow for young visitors and justify, noting a precaution.
questions.a: (a) Sun's focus heats the paper; the match is the heat source for the other. (b) The match: it is already hotter than the paper's ignition temperature. (c) Fuel and oxygen, and reaching the ignition temperature. (d) Either can be allowed with reason: lens has no flame but is slower; match is quick but has a flame; both under adult supervision.
s: Part (b): matchsticks hotter than ignition temperature
Part (c): fuel, oxygen and ignition temperature

questions.q:
(a) Name the three sides of the fire triangle.
(b) Which of these do focused sunrays supply to a sheet of paper?
questions.a: (a) Fuel, oxygen, heat. (b) Heat, bringing it to its ignition temperature.

questions.q:
A kadhai of oil on a gas stove flame catches fire in the school canteen. The cook can switch off the stove and cover the kadhai with a metal lid, or carry the burning kadhai outside. After 10 seconds under the lid, a helper lifts it to check and the flame returns.
(a) Name the fuel, the oxygen source and the heat source in the canteen fire.
(b) Which side does the lid remove?
(c) Why did the flame return when the lid was lifted?
(d) Decide between covering and carrying the kadhai outside, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Oil; air; the stove flame and hot kadhai. (b) Oxygen. (c) Fuel was still hot and air entered again. (d) Cover it and leave the lid on: carrying keeps fuel, heat and air together.
s: Part (c): air returned while heat remained

questions.q: A lighted matchstick is held to a sheet of paper and the paper catches fire almost at once. Why?
questions.a: The match is already above the ignition temperature of the paper.
o: The match is hotter than the ignition temperature of paper
The matchstick supplies the paper with the oxygen it needs
The paper has a higher ignition temperature than the match
Paper can only start burning when it directly touches a flame

questions.q: Anil expects the paper to catch fire the moment the focused sunray spot falls on it. Show why that cannot happen.
questions.a: Focusing heats the paper gradually; its temperature increases with time; it burns only after it reaches its ignition temperature, after giving out smoke.
s: Paper must reach ignition temperature first

questions.q: Describe a situation in which fuel and oxygen are both present, but there is no fire. Name the missing side and say how a fire could then start.
questions.a: e.g. Paper on a desk: heat is missing; holding a lighted match to it, or focusing sunrays, would bring it to its ignition temperature.
s: A valid situation with fuel and oxygen present
Names heat as the missing side
Says how a fire could start

questions.q: Dhruv holds a lighted matchstick to a small stone and to a sheet of paper, in the same room. Only the paper burns. Which requirement is missing for the stone?
questions.a: Oxygen and heat are the same for both; the stone is not a fuel.
o: A combustible substance (fuel)
Oxygen, since stones block the air
Heat, since a match is too cool for any substance
A flame larger than a match

questions.q:
A kadhai of oil catches fire on a gas stove.
(a) Which side of the fire triangle is removed by covering it with a lid?
(b) Which side would be removed by turning off the stove?
questions.a: (a) Oxygen (air supply). (b) Heat.

questions.q:
The school fire-safety card needs a rule for each situation: (a) oil burning in a canteen kadhai; (b) a heap of burning waste paper; (c) a person's clothes on fire.
(d) Name the side of the triangle each rule removes.
(e) Add one precaution from Activity 5.6.
questions.a: (a) Cover with a lid to cut off air. (b) Remove unburnt paper (fuel) or cover to cut off air. (c) Wrap a blanket to cut off air. Sides: oxygen, fuel/oxygen, oxygen. Precaution: do such activities with a teacher or adult.

questions.q:
Read the statements about combustion.
I. A substance can catch fire without a flame touching it, if it is heated enough.
II. A substance burns whenever fuel and oxygen are present, even without any heat.
III. If any one of fuel, oxygen or heat is removed, combustion stops.
questions.a: II is false: heat that reaches the ignition temperature is also needed.
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT needed for combustion?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide is a product, not a requirement.
o: A supply of carbon dioxide
A combustible substance (fuel)
Oxygen from the air
Heat to reach the ignition temperature

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes what happens to the wax of a lit candle?
questions.a: Melting, carried up the wick, evaporation and then burning of the vapour.
o: It melts, rises on the wick, evaporates and the vapour burns
It burns as a solid first, then melts and evaporates later
It evaporates first, then melts and then burns as a vapour
It melts, burns in its liquid form and then evaporates away

questions.q:
During a class activity three groups watch a lit candle for five minutes and note one thing each. Group P: wax near the wick turns into a clear liquid. Group Q: a yellow flame sits at the tip of the wick, and the wax near the wick slowly disappears. Group R: drops run down the sides and become a white solid at the base.
(a) Name the change P noted and its type.
(b) What exactly burns in the flame Q saw, and what type of change is it?
(c) Name the change R noted and its type.
(d) Two groups argue over whether burning a candle is physical or chemical. Decide, naming which groups' notes support each side.
questions.a: (a) Melting, physical. (b) Wax vapour; chemical. (c) Solidifying, physical. (d) Both: P and R support physical, Q supports chemical.
s: Part (d): both kinds, matching groups to sides

questions.q: What actually burns to give the flame of a candle?
questions.a: Wax melts, is carried up the wick and evaporates; its vapour burns.
o: The vapour of the wax
The solid wax at the base of the candle
The cotton thread of the wick alone
The melted wax collected in the pool

questions.q:
(a) What carries melted wax up to the flame?
(b) What happens to the wax at the top of the wick because of the heat of the flame?
questions.a: (a) The wick. (b) It evaporates, and the vapour burns.
s: Part (b): evaporation and burning of vapour

questions.q:
Sneha lit a wax candle in a lantern on Diwali night. After an hour the candle was shorter and a ring of hard wax had formed at its base. Her brother wants to collect the hard wax and melt it to make a new candle. Her mother says burning a candle is completely reversible, so no wax will be lost.
(a) Name the physical changes that took place.
(b) What burned to make the flame?
(c) Why did the candle become shorter?
(d) Decide what can and cannot be recovered from the candle.
questions.a: (a) Melting, solidifying, evaporation. (b) Wax vapour. (c) Wax melted, evaporated and the vapour burned. (d) The hard wax can be remelted; the wax that burned formed new substances and cannot be got back.
s: Part (d): ring recoverable; burned wax not

questions.q: Asha says burning a candle is only a physical change, Bilal says it is only a chemical change, and Chitra says it involves both. Whose view matches the chapter?
questions.a: Both kinds of change occur.
o: Chitra's: melting is physical and burning the vapour is chemical
Asha's, since wax only changes its state when it melts
Bilal's, since new substances form at every single stage
Asha and Bilal together, as each describes the whole candle

questions.q: Rohan says: 'The flame of a candle comes from burning wax vapour, not from solid wax.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. Wax melts, rises along the wick and evaporates due to the heat of the flame; the vapour burns to produce the flame.
s: The vapour burns, producing the flame

questions.q:
A candle is burning.
(a) Name the physical changes of the wax.
(b) Why is the burning of wax vapour called a chemical change?
questions.a: (a) Melting, solidifying and evaporation. (b) New substances are formed.

questions.q:
Explain the sequence from lighting a candle to its flame.
(a) Describe each stage.
(b) Label each as physical or chemical.
(c) Explain why the whole candle is said to involve both kinds of change.
questions.a: Wick heated; wax melts; carried up the wick; evaporates; vapour burns. Melting and evaporation are physical; burning is chemical.

questions.q:
Three students discuss a burning candle. Imran says, 'The wick itself is what burns.' Joy says, 'The vapour of the wax burns.' Kriti says, 'Solid wax burns directly.'
(a) Evaluate each statement against the chapter.
(b) Say which statements are true but incomplete, and which are wrong.
(c) Give the complete picture.
questions.a: Imran: wrong, the wick carries the liquid wax. Joy: right but incomplete without melting and evaporation. Kriti: wrong, vapour burns. Complete: melts, rises, evaporates, vapour burns.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Burning a candle involves both physical and chemical changes.
Reason (R): Wax melts and evaporates before its vapour burns.
questions.a: Both are true; melting and evaporation are physical and the burning of vapour is chemical, which explains the assertion.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: Who was Michael Faraday, and what did he discuss through a candle?
questions.a: A scientist who delivered Chemical History of a Candle in the nineteenth century, discussing melting, vapourisation and combustion.

questions.q: A candle becomes noticeably shorter after burning for an hour, though only a little wax has collected below it. Which best explains the missing wax?
questions.a: Wax melts, evaporates and its vapour burns to form new substances.
o: Much of it evaporated and its vapour burned
All of it melted and soaked permanently into the wick material
It turned straight from solid wax into the flame itself
It evaporated and spread into the room without ever burning

questions.q: Michael Faraday's nineteenth-century series of lectures was called
questions.a: Book: Chemical History of a Candle.
o: Chemical History of a Candle
Physical History of a Candle and Wax
The Candle and its Bright Flame
The Chemical Nature of Fire and Light

questions.q: Which process in a burning candle is a chemical change?
questions.a: Melting, solidifying and evaporation are physical; burning the vapour forms new substances.
o: The burning of wax vapour
The melting of wax near the wick
The solidifying of wax drops at the base
The evaporation of wax by the heat of the flame

questions.q: Write a short record of what a student sees in five minutes at a lit candle, including two physical changes and one chemical change. Label each.
questions.a: e.g. Wax near wick melts (physical). Drops harden at the base (physical). Flame forms from burning vapour (chemical).
s: Each linked to a correct reason

questions.q: At a birthday party, wax drips from a candle onto the edge of a cake plate and hardens into small beads. Which statement describes this?
questions.a: Melting and solidifying form no new substance.
o: Melting followed by solidifying, which are physical changes
Burning of wax, which is a chemical change
A reaction between wax and the plate forming a new substance
Evaporation of wax, which is a chemical change

questions.q:
Wax drops harden at the base of a candle.
(a) Name the change.
(b) The hardened wax is melted again by warming; what does that show about the change?
questions.a: (a) Solidifying, a physical change. (b) It can be reversed; no new substance formed.

questions.q: Classify as physical or chemical: (i) a pool of wax forms, (ii) wax rises in the wick, (iii) the flame forms, (iv) wax drops harden, (v) the candle becomes shorter.
questions.a: Physical: (i), (ii), (iv). Chemical: (iii). (v) is due to evaporation and burning together.

questions.q: Differentiate between the melting of wax and the burning of wax vapour.
questions.a: Melting: physical, solid to liquid, no new substance. Burning of vapour: chemical, new substances form with heat and light.
s: Burning described as chemical with new substances

questions.q:
Read the statements about a burning candle.
I. The wick helps carry melted wax upwards.
II. Melting, solidifying and evaporation of wax are physical changes.
III. Burning of wax vapour is a chemical change.
questions.a: All three are true.
o: Statements I, II and III
Statements I and II only
Statements II and III only
Statements I and III only

questions.q: Define a reversible and an irreversible change with one example each.
questions.a: Reversible: original substance can be got back, e.g. ice. Irreversible: cannot, e.g. popcorn.

questions.q: Write a short story of three or four lines that includes compost, rusting and ripening. Label each change desirable or undesirable.
questions.a: e.g. Peels become compost (desirable); the gate rusts (undesirable); mangoes ripen (desirable).
s: Each label linked to a reason

questions.q: Which pair contains one reversible and one irreversible change?
questions.a: Condensing vapour can be reversed, popcorn cannot. Each other pair is both-reversible or both-irreversible.
o: Condensing water vapour; making popcorn
Melting ice; condensing water vapour
Chopping vegetables; forming soil from rocks
Making popcorn; chopping vegetables

questions.q:
A society has: (i) kitchen waste in a pit, (ii) an iron gate rusting, (iii) milk turning into curd, (iv) food spoiling on a shelf.
(a) Classify each as desirable or undesirable.
(b) Which two are the same kind of change but need opposite decisions?
(c) Which change is the chapter's example of a chemical change?
(d) Decide which one needs action first and justify.
questions.a: (i) desirable; (ii) undesirable; (iii) desirable; (iv) undesirable. (b) (i) and (iv): decay. (c) Rusting. (d) Rusting or spoilage with reason.

questions.q: Differentiate between desirable and undesirable changes with one example each.
questions.a: Desirable: useful, e.g. milk into curd. Undesirable: harmful, e.g. rusting.

questions.q: Painters repaint the school walls. As the paint dries, strong smells spread in the corridor. Which concern fits the chapter?
questions.a: Drying of paint releases substances causing atmospheric pollution.
o: Drying releases substances into the air, causing pollution
Drying paint is reversible, so nothing remains in the air
Drying paint absorbs the carbon dioxide from the room air
Evaporation of paint is a desirable change in every situation

questions.q:
(a) Give one change in a kitchen that can be reversed.
(b) Give one that cannot, and say what you cannot get back.
questions.a: (a) Melting ice (refreeze it). (b) Chopping vegetables; the original size and shape.
s: Part (b): irreversible change and what is lost

questions.q:
In Meenakshi's housing society, kitchen waste is put in a pit at the back of the compound and, after some weeks, is used as compost for the garden. Residents of the nearest block complain about the smell from the pit. The iron gate has brown patches, and food kept in the hall's storage room spoiled last month.
(a) Is the change in the pit desirable or undesirable? Explain.
(b) Name the change on the gate.
(c) Why is spoilage in the storage room undesirable though the same decay is useful in the pit?
(d) The secretary must choose: keep the pit but move it away from houses, or close it and send waste away. Decide.
questions.a: (a) Desirable: waste becomes compost. (b) Rusting; undesirable. (c) The food is wasted in storage; in the pit it is used. (d) Keep the pit but move it, to keep the useful change and reduce the smell.

questions.q: Give two ways in which human activity causes long-term changes in the environment, naming the substance involved.
questions.a: More fuel burned raises carbon dioxide; drying paint releases substances that pollute the air.

questions.q: A cook says: ice refrozen, onions chopped, corn made into popcorn and steam condensed. Which pair of these changes cannot be reversed?
questions.a: Chopped onions and popcorn cannot go back.
o: Chopping the onions and making popcorn
Refreezing the ice and condensing the steam
Chopping the onions and refreezing the ice
Making the popcorn and condensing the steam

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a desirable change?
questions.a: Rusting is undesirable; the others are useful.
o: Rusting of an iron gate
Cooking dal on a stove
Milk turning into curd
Cutting fruits for a salad

questions.q: A student says a change is either desirable or undesirable, never both. Show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: Decay of food is undesirable in storage but desirable when waste becomes compost; the same change can be both depending on situation.

questions.q: Which of these changes can be reversed?
questions.a: Ice can be refrozen. The other three cannot go back.
o: Melting ice and refreezing it
Chopping vegetables into small pieces
Making popcorn from corn
Forming soil from rocks

questions.q: Reena's mother puts vegetable peels into a pit and, after some weeks, they become compost for the garden. Which statement fits?
questions.a: Decomposition of food waste into compost is useful.
o: Decay that is unwelcome in stored food is useful here
Decomposition is undesirable in every situation, even here
The peels can be got back, so it is a reversible change
The peels stay peels, so it is only a physical change

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. A change that is undesirable in one situation can never be desirable in another.
II. Rusting of iron is an undesirable change.
III. Turning food waste into compost is a desirable change.
questions.a: I is false: decay of food is undesirable in storage but desirable when making compost.
o: Statements II and III only
Statements I and II only
Statements I and III only
Statements I, II and III

questions.q: Increased consumption of fuels in cars, trains and aeroplanes
questions.a: Burning more fuel adds carbon dioxide.
o: is raising carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
is raising the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere
is lowering carbon dioxide since combustion is physical
has no long-term effect on the atmosphere over the years

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Refreezing melted ice
2. Making popcorn from corn
3. Food waste turning into compost
4. Burning more fuel in vehicles
A. A change that cannot be reversed
B. A change that can be reversed
C. Raises carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
D. Decay made useful
questions.a: Refreezing ice: reversible (B); popcorn: cannot be reversed (A); compost: useful decay (D); fuel burning raises carbon dioxide (C).

questions.q: Tara says: 'Decomposition is always undesirable, because rusting and decay of stored food are undesirable.' Do you agree? Give an example.
questions.a: No. Decomposition of food waste into compost is useful, so a change can be undesirable in one situation and desirable in another.
s: Situation decides whether a change is desirable

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Melting of ice is a reversible change.
Reason (R): Water vapour can be condensed back to water.
questions.a: Both are true. R is another example of a reversible change; it does not explain why ice can be refrozen.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q:
Write a short note on how human activity causes long-term changes.
(a) Give the first example and its effect.
(b) Give the second example and its effect.
(c) Link each to a chapter idea (combustion or evaporation).
(d) Suggest one thing a school can do.
questions.a: More fuel in vehicles raises carbon dioxide. Drying paint releases substances by evaporation causing pollution. A school can reduce fuel use or limit painting.

questions.q:
(a) Why is the decay of stored food undesirable?
(b) How does the same decomposition become desirable?
questions.a: (a) It spoils the food. (b) Food waste decomposes into compost.

questions.q:
Aman uses 4 litres of petrol a week on his scooter, and his shop wall is repainted every two years. His shop's ice slab melts by evening, and he makes popcorn for customers. He can cycle to the shop and save the 4 litres each week, or repaint every four years instead of two.
(a) Which change in the stem can be reversed?
(b) How many litres of petrol would be saved in a year of 52 weeks?
(c) Which two actions have an environmental impact, and what is it?
(d) Decide which choice reduces more of the burning-fuel effect and justify.
questions.a: (a) Melting ice (can be refrozen). (b) 4 x 52 = 208 litres. (c) Burning fuel raises carbon dioxide; drying paint releases pollutants. (d) Cycling: fuel is burnt every week, so it affects the atmosphere more often.
s: Part (c): fuel and paint with effects
Part (d): reasoned decision using the numbers

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Weathering includes both physical and chemical changes in rocks.
II. Erosion can be caused by wind or flowing water.
III. The changes of weathering and erosion finish in a few days and can be reversed.
questions.a: III is false: these changes take thousands of years and cannot be reversed.
o: Both I and II, but not III
Both II and III, but not I
Both I and III, but not II
All of I, II and III

questions.q: The red layer on the surface of black basalt is due to
questions.a: Basalt contains iron; long exposure to water or moist air gives iron oxide.
o: iron oxide formed on long exposure to moist air
paint carried by rain over the rock surface for years
tree roots growing into the cracks of the rock
freezing of water in the cracks of the rock

questions.q:
(a) What are sediments?
(b) How would sediments at the base of a mountain differ from the rock they came from?
questions.a: (a) Sand, soil and stones. (b) They are smaller pieces of the large rock, broken off by physical changes.
s: Part (b): smaller pieces from large rock

questions.q:
(a) Name two physical causes that break rocks.
(b) Why does a rock containing iron turn red after long exposure to moist air?
questions.a: (a) Temperature changes, growing roots, freezing water in cracks. (b) Iron oxide forms in a chemical change.

questions.q: A contractor promises that the sediments from a landslide can be pressed back into solid rock in a week. Show why this cannot work.
questions.a: Sediments harden into rocks only over thousands of years, and these changes cannot be reversed.
s: A week does not match this

questions.q: A muddy river enters a calm lake and silt settles on the bottom. After thousands of years, the layers have hardened. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Material settles when speed decreases; sediments harden over thousands of years.
o: Sediments settle as water slows, then harden into rock
Erosion makes new rocks directly within a few years
Weathering carries the silt into the lake over time
Wind erosion has made the rocks, and the change is quickly reversible

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Erosion by flowing water is a physical change.
Reason (R): Erosion converts rocks into soil by a chemical reaction with water.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: forming soil is weathering; erosion only breaks down and moves material.
o: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: Which statement about erosion is NOT correct?
questions.a: Erosion in a landslide is a physical change.
o: Erosion during a landslide is a chemical change
River pebbles look smooth because of constant erosion
Material settles when water or wind slows down
Wind can move sediments from one place to another

questions.q: Write three or four lines of a news item about a hillside that includes weathering, erosion and settling of sediments, in that order.
questions.a: e.g. Frost splits rock on the slope (weathering); a stream carries the pieces down (erosion); at the pond they settle (sediments).

questions.q: Erosion is the
questions.a: Weathering forms soil; erosion moves material.
o: moving of pebbles, soil and sediments by wind and flowing water
slow formation of soil from rocks by physical and chemical changes
settling and hardening of sediments into new rocks
chemical change of basalt into a red layer over a long time

questions.q: Sediments such as sand, soil and stones at the base of mountains are formed when
questions.a: Book: sediments form by physical changes breaking up large rocks.
o: large rocks break into smaller pieces by physical changes
new rocks harden after many layers settle in a lake
iron oxide turns the surface of the rocks red
water vapour condenses on cool rocks at night

questions.q: A banyan seed sprouts in a crack of an old stone fort wall and, after many years, the crack is wider and pieces of stone have fallen off. What does this show?
questions.a: Growing roots of trees are a cause of physical changes that break rocks.
o: Growing roots can break rock, a physical weathering change
Roots cause erosion by moving the stones with flowing water
Roots turn the rock into iron oxide by a chemical change
Roots harden the loose sediments into new rock layers

questions.q: What happens to sediments carried by water when the water slows down, and what do they become over time?
questions.a: They settle at the bottom and, over time, harden into new rocks.

questions.q: Differentiate between weathering and erosion.
questions.a: Weathering breaks and changes rocks by physical and chemical changes leading to soil. Erosion moves broken material by wind or flowing water.

questions.q:
A river runs fast through hills and its water is brown with soil. Near a village the water slows in a reservoir, where a 2 cm layer of silt settles each year. The village committee must choose a site for a new pump house: Site X on the fast stretch of the river or Site Y on the bank of the reservoir.
(a) Name the process that carried the soil downstream.
(b) Why does silt settle at the reservoir?
(c) How thick will the silt layer be after 15 years, and what happens over thousands of years?
(d) Decide which site is more exposed to erosion, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Erosion by flowing water. (b) The speed of the water decreases. (c) 2 x 15 = 30 cm; it hardens into new rock. (d) Site X: fast water moves more material.

questions.q: Define weathering and state what it eventually leads to.
questions.a: The physical and chemical changes in rocks; it leads to formation of soil.

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Sediments
2. Erosion
3. Weathering
4. Basalt turning red
A. Physical and chemical changes in rocks that lead to soil
B. Moving of pebbles, soil and sediments by wind and flowing water
C. Chemical change producing iron oxide
D. Sand, soil and stones at the base of mountains
questions.a: Sediments: sand, soil, stones (D); erosion: moving material (B); weathering: leads to soil (A); basalt turning red: iron oxide (C).

questions.q:
Village A is on a bare steep slope with fast streams. Village B is on a gentle slope beside a calm lake where streams slow down.
(a) Which village is more at risk from erosion?
(b) Where would sediments settle?
(c) What happens to these sediments over thousands of years?
(d) Decide which village needs more care for its slope, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Village A, as fast water and wind move material. (b) Near the calm lake in Village B. (c) They harden into new rocks. (d) Village A needs more care to reduce erosion.

questions.q: Ketan picks round smooth pebbles from a riverbed and rough stones from the hillside. Why are the river pebbles smooth?
questions.a: The book says river rocks and pebbles are smoother because of constant erosion by flowing water.
o: Flowing water has kept rubbing them: erosion
The river chemically changes the pebbles into a new substance
Roots of trees have grown around them for many years
Sediments have hardened into new rocks around them

questions.q: Ritu says: 'Weathering of rocks can involve chemical changes as well as physical ones.' Do you agree? Give an example of each.
questions.a: Yes. Physical: temperature changes, growing roots or freezing water. Chemical: iron-containing basalt forming red iron oxide with water or moist air.

questions.q:
On a trip to the Uttarakhand foothills, students found sand, soil and stones at the base of a steep slope. The guide showed a black rock with a red layer on its surface, and said a landslide after heavy rain had moved earth downhill. In the nearby river they found smooth round pebbles. The class can collect samples from only one place, either the base of the cliff or the riverbed.
(a) How were the sand and stones at the base formed?
(b) Name the substance in the red layer and the type of change.
(c) What do we call the movement of earth in the landslide, and what kind of change is it?
(d) Decide which place gives samples that best show erosion at work, and why.
questions.a: (a) Large rocks broke by physical changes. (b) Iron oxide; chemical. (c) Erosion; physical. (d) The riverbed: smooth pebbles result from constant erosion by flowing water.

questions.q:
Trace a rock on a mountain to a new rock.
(a) Describe the stages.
(b) Say which stage is weathering and which is erosion.
(c) Label each as physical or chemical.
(d) State whether the journey can be reversed.
questions.a: Rock breaks (weathering) into sediments; wind and water move them (erosion); they settle; they harden into new rocks. Weathering is physical and chemical; erosion is physical; it cannot be reversed.
